content.title: About
content.content: A meat‑free bao bun is a soft steamed Asian roll made from wheat flour, yeast, sugar and water. It is typically filled with vegetables, tofu, mushrooms or other plant‑based ingredients, making it a popular vegetarian and vegan option.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bao buns originated in Jiangsu province, China, where they were traditionally served as a snack.
The dough is egg‑free, so it can easily be adapted for a vegan diet.
Steaming preserves most nutrients and gives the bun its characteristic pillowy texture.
In Japan similar buns are called “hanomachi,” and in Taiwan they are known as “pao‑bo.”
Bao buns are often served with soy sauce, chili oil or pickled vegetables.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The dough is mainly carbohydrate with only a small amount of plant oil, making the dish light when eaten in moderation.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Vegetable and legume fillings add dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Tofu, tempeh or mushrooms provide a complete set of amino acids for vegetarians.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Yeast‑based dough supplies vitamins B1, B2 and B3, which help energy metabolism.

items.title: Low glycemic impact
items.content: Steaming and the combination with vegetables slow sugar absorption, beneficial for blood‑glucose control.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The dough contains wheat flour, so people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should choose a gluten‑free version.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Accompanying sauces are often salty; it’s advisable to use them sparingly.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: If the filling includes tofu, it must be stored and reheated properly to prevent bacterial growth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bao buns are usually split open and filled with hot vegetables, tofu, marinated mushrooms or bean sprouts. They can be eaten by hand as a street‑food snack or with a fork and knife.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked buns in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. To restore softness, re‑steam or microwave them briefly before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Brandy is a distilled spirit made by double‑distilling fermented grape wine. It boasts a rich aroma, deep flavor, and a characteristic golden‑amber hue. Many brandies are aged in oak barrels, which impart notes of vanilla, caramel, and spice.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “brandy” comes from the Dutch “brandewijn,” meaning “burnt wine.”
The most famous type of brandy is Cognac, produced in a strictly defined region of France.
Traditionally, brandy is served in small snifters that allow its aromas to fully develop.
In some cuisines, brandy is used for flambéing desserts and sauces.
Aging in oak can last from a few years to several decades, influencing taste and price.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Polyphenols and other compounds in brandy may help neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: A modest amount of brandy after a meal is traditionally believed to support digestion.

items.title: Improves circulation
items.content: Ethanol in small doses can dilate blood vessels, enhancing blood flow.

items.title: Alcohol dependence
items.content: Excessive consumption of brandy can lead to addiction and liver damage.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Alcohol may amplify the effects of certain medications, including sedatives and anticoagulants.

items.title: Pregnancy and lactation
items.content: Alcohol intake is contraindicated during pregnancy and while breastfeeding.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Brandy is typically served in small glasses at room temperature. It can be enjoyed neat, on the rocks, or in cocktails. For a fragrant experience, let the spirit breathe in the glass for a few minutes before sipping.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep brandy in a tightly sealed bottle, away from direct sunlight and temperature fluctuations. After opening, store the bottle in a cool place, but not in the refrigerator, to preserve its aroma.

content.title: About
content.content: Fluid replacement, electrolyte solution (5528) is designed for rapid rehydration and electrolyte replenishment during dehydration, diarrhea, intense exercise, or heat exposure. It contains sodium, potassium, chloride, magnesium, and glucose to provide effective hydration and maintain acid‑base balance.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The formulation follows WHO guidelines for oral rehydration solutions.
Glucose enhances sodium absorption in the gut via co‑transport mechanisms.
The solution can be used in medical settings as well as field conditions such as sports events.
Each 250 ml serving supplies about 75 % of an adult's daily sodium requirement.
The product contains no artificial colors or flavors.

items.title: Rapid fluid replenishment
items.content: The combination of electrolytes and glucose speeds up water absorption in the intestine, helping quickly restore extracellular fluid volume.

items.title: Electrolyte balance support
items.content: Sodium, potassium, and magnesium aid normal nerve and muscle function, preventing cramps and weakness.

items.title: Reduced risk of hypovolemia
items.content: Regular intake during fluid loss helps avoid drops in blood pressure and impaired circulation.

items.title: Improved recovery after exercise
items.content: Electrolytes facilitate faster muscle recovery and lessen feelings of fatigue.

items.title: Acid‑base balance maintenance
items.content: The solution helps keep blood pH within normal range when bicarbonate is lost through sweat.

items.title: Hypernatremia
items.content: Excessive consumption may raise blood sodium levels, especially in individuals with kidney disease or heart failure.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Rare allergic reactions can occur to excipients such as flavorings or preservatives.

items.title: Not suitable for hyperkalemia
items.content: People with high blood potassium should limit intake of the solution.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Glucose raises the glycemic index; diabetics should monitor the amount consumed.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Dissolve one packet (or tablet) in 250 ml of clean water. Drink small sips every 5–10 minutes over 1–2 hours or as directed by a healthcare professional. More frequent dosing may be needed for severe dehydration.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and use within 24 hours. Discard if the package is damaged or the solution changes color or odor.

content.title: About
content.content: Sesame chicken is a popular Asian‑inspired dish consisting of bite‑size pieces of chicken breast coated in a light batter, fried until crisp, and tossed in a sweet‑tangy sauce with toasted sesame seeds. The result is tender meat, a crunchy exterior, and a fragrant nutty flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in Chinese-American restaurants and has become a staple in many fast‑food menus worldwide.
Sesame seeds are rich in calcium, magnesium, and lignans, which are natural antioxidants.
The sauce typically combines soy sauce, honey or sugar, rice vinegar, ginger, and garlic for its characteristic sweet‑sour profile.
Traditional recipes marinate the chicken in soy sauce and rice wine before coating and frying.
Both white and black sesame seeds can be used; black sesame adds a deeper, earthier aroma.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken breast provides lean protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Sesame seeds contain mono‑ and polyunsaturated fatty acids that support heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken and soy sauce supply B6 and B12 vitamins, important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Sesame contributes calcium, iron, and magnesium, beneficial for bones and nerve function.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Lignans and vitamin E in sesame help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Sesame allergy
items.content: Sesame is a major allergen; sensitive individuals may experience severe reactions.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce adds a lot of salt, which can be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Added sugars
items.content: Sweet sauces increase calories and can affect blood glucose levels.

items.title: Frying oil
items.content: Deep‑frying adds extra calories and may introduce trans fats if the oil is reused.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve sesame chicken hot, sprinkled with toasted seeds, alongside rice, noodles, or stir‑fried vegetables. Garnish with sliced green onions or cilantro for extra freshness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat in a skillet to retain the crispness of the coating.

stewed-seasoned-ground-beef-and-pork-wit.title: Stewed, seasoned, ground beef and pork with potatoes, Mexican style

content.title: About
content.content: Stewed, seasoned, ground beef and pork with potatoes in Mexican style is a hearty dish that combines tender ground beef and pork, aromatic Mexican spices, and potatoes baked to a golden crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional Mexican seasoning blends often include chili, cumin, and oregano for a distinctive flavor.
A mix of beef and pork gives a softer texture and richer taste than using a single meat.
Potatoes are usually par‑fried before being stewed with the meat, allowing them to soak up the spices.
The dish is commonly served with lime, fresh cilantro, and guacamole for bright contrast.
In the United States it is frequently sold as a frozen ready‑to‑heat meal in supermarkets.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Beef and pork provide complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Red meat supplies heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat is a good source of B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Potassium from potatoes
items.content: Potatoes contribute potassium, which helps maintain normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Antioxidants from spices
items.content: Chili and other spices contain capsaicin and polyphenols with anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Beef and pork contain saturated fats that can raise cholesterol if consumed in excess.

items.title: Salt and heat
items.content: The dish can be high in sodium and spicy peppers, which may be problematic for hypertension or spice‑sensitive individuals.

items.title: Spice allergies
items.content: Some people may be allergic to specific spices such as coriander or cumin.

items.title: Thorough cooking required
items.content: Ground meat must be cooked to a safe internal temperature to avoid food‑borne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot, often alongside rice, corn tortillas, or fresh vegetables. Add lime juice, sour cream, guacamole, or shredded cheese to enhance the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze portions for 2‑3 months. Reheat until the internal temperature reaches at least 75 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: Table fat NFS (Non‑Frying Substance) is a food-grade fat derived from vegetable oils, specially processed for culinary and food‑industry use. It has a neutral taste, high heat stability, and is suitable for frying, baking, and sauce preparation.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Table fat is widely used in restaurants and cafeterias because of its uniform texture and predictable cooking behavior.
NFS fats can be produced from various vegetable sources such as soy, sunflower, and rapeseed oil.
Unlike butter, table fat contains no dairy proteins, making it suitable for people with lactose intolerance.
It has a higher smoke point than many vegetable oils, allowing use at higher temperatures.
In some countries, table fat is classified as a “food product without added flavorings” (NFS).

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Fats provide a concentrated source of calories, supplying the body with energy for prolonged physical activity.

items.title: Contains essential fatty acids
items.content: Depending on the source oil, table fat can supply linoleic and alpha‑linolenic acids, essential for healthy cell membranes.

items.title: Supports vitamin absorption
items.content: Fats enhance the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K.

items.title: Cooking stability
items.content: A high smoke point reduces the formation of harmful oxidation products during frying.

items.title: Free of trans fats
items.content: Modern processing allows production of table fat without trans fats, making it a safer option for cardiovascular health.

items.title: High caloric density
items.content: Like all fats, table fat is calorie‑dense, so intake should be moderated.

items.title: Allergy to vegetable oils
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to the source oils (soy, sunflower, etc.).

items.title: Oxidation during storage
items.content: If stored for long periods, the fat can oxidize and develop an off‑odor; keep it in a cool, dark place.

items.title: May contain animal emulsifiers
items.content: Certain variants might include trace animal‑derived emulsifiers; check the label if you follow a vegan diet.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Table fat is suitable for frying, baking, making sauces, marinades, and dough. It can replace butter in recipes where a neutral flavor and high cooking temperature are desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store table fat in a tightly sealed container in a cool, dry, dark place. For extended shelf life, keep it refrigerated to prevent oxidation. Discard the product if it develops an unusual smell or color.

content.title: About
content.content: Tripe is the edible stomach lining (usually from cattle, pigs or sheep). It has a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a pleasantly firm texture when cooked. Tripe is used in many traditional dishes around the world.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tripe is considered a delicacy in many countries, including France (tripes à la mode), China and Mexico.
In ancient Roman cuisine, tripe was served in soups and stews.
Tripe is rich in collagen, which is also used in cosmetic products.
In some cultures tripe is called “poor man’s meat”, yet gourmet chefs prepare it with refined sauces.
There are several types of tripe – honeycomb, blanket, book, etc., named after the part of the stomach.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Tripe provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Tripe is a good source of iron, zinc and selenium, important for immunity and blood formation.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many other meat products, tripe has a moderate fat content.

items.title: Supports skin health
items.content: The collagen in tripe helps maintain skin elasticity and repair.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: If not cooked thoroughly, tripe can harbor bacteria and parasites.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to animal offal.

items.title: High cholesterol
items.content: Tripe contains cholesterol, so people with cardiovascular issues should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: Its dense texture can be hard to digest, especially when undercooked.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tripe is usually cleaned, boiled and sliced. It is used in soups, stews, stir‑fries, salads and ground into patties. Soaking it in cold water with a splash of vinegar before cooking helps reduce any strong odor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh tripe refrigerated at 0‑4 °C and use within 2‑3 days. Frozen tripe can be stored in an airtight bag for up to 3 months.
